Abstract—Uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) have become essen-
tial in advancing multiaccess edge computing (MEC), providing
ﬂexible platforms that enhance network capacity, coverage, and
efﬁciency while reducing latency and improving communication
quality. Integrating reconﬁgurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) with
UAV-based MEC systems further elevates these capabilities, deliv-
ering signiﬁcant gains in computational power, energy efﬁciency
(EE), and physical-layer security (PLS). However, managing the
complexity of RIS within UAV networks requires sophisticated
optimization strategies. This survey offers a comprehensive
analysis of the fundamentals of RIS, UAVs, and MEC, followed
by an in-depth examination of RIS conﬁgurations in UAV-based
MEC systems, including static, dynamic, and hybrid models. We
evaluate the beneﬁts and challenges of RIS integration, such
as improved communication, enhanced computational efﬁciency,
optimized energy use, better task management, and strengthened
security. In addition, the survey explores the latest advancements
in RIS-assisted UAVs for MEC, focusing on boosting computa-
tional capacity, minimizing delay, maximizing EE, and enhancing
security. To provide a thorough exploration of these topics,
detailed summary tables are included, offering a comparative
analysis of methodologies, performance metrics, and scenarios
from recent studies. Furthermore, the survey presents key lessons

I. INTRODUCTION
T
HE EXPLOSIVE growth of the Internet of Things (IoT)
has led to a surge in data generation, driving the need for
more effective computational and communication frameworks.
Multiaccess edge computing (MEC) addresses this demand
by bringing data processing closer to the data’s origin, at
the network edge [1]. This proximity greatly reduces latency,
which is essential for real-time applications like autonomous
vehicles, smart cities, and industrial automation. MEC also
optimizes bandwidth usage by processing data locally, reduc-
ing the need to transmit large volumes of data to central
cloud data centers [2]. By shifting computational tasks to
edge servers, MEC not only eases the load on core networks
but also enhances overall network performance, scalability,
and resilience, making it a vital component in the IoT
ecosystem [3].
Expanding on MEC’s capabilities, uncrewed aerial vehi-
cles (UAVs) have become vital in enhancing MEC systems,
offering UAV-mounted and UAV-enabled solutions that signif-
icantly improve computational and communication capacities
in challenging environments. UAV-mounted MEC focuses on
integrating MEC infrastructure directly onto UAVs, enabling
real-time processing and reduced latency, particularly ben-
eﬁcial in scenarios requiring rapid deployment and high
mobility [4]. However, this approach faces limitations due to
the UAV’s physical constraints, such as limited battery life
and payload capacity [5]. On the other hand, UAV-enabled
MEC provides a more ﬂexible and scalable framework by
integrating UAVs into a broader MEC network [6]. In this
setup, UAVs can either process data locally or act as relays
to other computing nodes, optimizing resource allocation,
extending coverage to remote or underserved regions, and
minimizing latency by processing data closer to users [7]. The
dual capability of UAV-enabled MEC renders it particularly
advantageous in dynamic circumstances, including disaster
response, rural locations, and metropolitan regions, where
ground infrastructure may be deﬁcient or impaired [8]. Despite
these advantages, UAV-enabled MEC systems must navigate

RISs have introduced transformative capabilities in wireless
communication by providing ﬁne-grained control over electro-

be dynamically adjusted to optimize aspects, such as signal

RIS can be especially beneﬁcial in environments where line-
of-sight (LoS) is obstructed or where signal strength is weak.
In such situations, RIS can be used to optimize signal paths,
reﬂecting or refracting signals around obstacles, ensuring
strong and reliable communication links [13]. This capability
proves particularly valuable for UAVs operating in complex,
dynamic environments. For UAVs, the integration of RIS offers
signiﬁcant advantages in terms of communication reliability,
EE, and computational load. By improving the efﬁciency
of signal transmission, RIS reduces the need for intensive
on-board processing, conserving power, and extending ﬂight
times, which is crucial for missions, such as surveillance and
remote sensing [14]. Additionally, RIS can optimize signal
paths to ensure UAVs maintain strong communication links
without expending excessive energy, directly contributing to
longer operational periods and reduced operational costs [15].

communication and computing services, enhancing both the
efﬁciency and reliability of IoT ecosystems. This synergy not

A. Related Surveys Comparisons
While extensive research has been conducted on RIS and its
applications, as documented in numerous reviews and tutorials
summarized in Table I, our survey diverges by focusing
speciﬁcally on the integration of RIS with UAVs to empower
MEC—a topic not thoroughly addressed in the existing lit-
erature. This study offers new perspectives and deepens the
understanding of RIS-aided UAVs in enhancing edge com-
puting environments, thereby addressing a critical gap. Our
approach provides a comprehensive overview that integrates
both well-established knowledge and emerging trends in RIS
technology.
The concept of RIS has not been investigated in prior works,
such as [21], [22], [23], and [24]. The paper referenced in [21]
provides a basic overview of UAV and MEC technologies,
with a speciﬁc focus on EE and a brief discussion on the
ofﬂoading possibilities within UAV-assisted MEC networks.
Additionally, Michailidis et al. [22] reviewed security solu-
tions for UAV-aided MEC-enabled IoT, exploring advanced
security methodologies and information-theoretic techniques

The surveys cited in [25], [26], [27], [28], and [29] did
not include the MEC system in their studies. The study

communication systems, focusing on important performance

II. FUNDAMENTALS OF RIS, UAV, AND MEC
In this section, we present an overview of RIS, a ground-
breaking technology in wireless communication. RIS can
be classiﬁed into passive, active, and hybrid types, each
capable of actively manipulating electromagnetic waves to
enhance signal propagation and network efﬁciency. These
programmable metasurfaces provide precise control over
waveforms, improving signal quality in challenging environ-
ments by redirecting and focusing signals toward intended
receivers. Overall, RIS technology, with its dual transmitting
and receiving modes, offers diverse solutions for enhancing
wireless networks by improving network adaptability and
efﬁciency.
A. Overview of RIS
RIS technology marks a signiﬁcant advancement in wireless
communication. These surfaces are embedded with numerous
miniature elements capable of manipulating electromagnetic
waves, thus enhancing signal propagation [30]. RIS is cate-
gorized into three main types: 1) passive RIS; 2) active RIS;
and 3) hybrid RIS. Their central functionalities include signal
reﬂection, refraction, and the innovative STAR-RIS approach.
By dynamically manipulating electromagnetic waves, RIS
improves signal direction, strength, and interference control,
enhancing wireless communications [31]. Applications of
RIS span various domains, from network efﬁciency improve-
ments to secure communications. Each type of RISpassive,
active, and STAR-RISoffers distinct advantages, such as
improved network performance, lower power consumption,
and enhanced signal coverage [32].
Despite the transformative potential of RIS technology in
WNs, challenges persist. These include intricate hardware
design, seamless integration with existing network infrastruc-
tures, and the development of sophisticated control algorithms.
Researchers are actively addressing these obstacles to fully
harness RIS capabilities for advancing efﬁcient wireless com-
munication systems [33]. Fig. 2 illustrates the three types
of RIS: 1) passive RIS; 2) active RIS; and 3) hybrid
RIS.
1) Passive RIS: Passive RIS utilizes cost-effective mate-
rials in various applications, such as building facades and
wearable technology, to bolster wireless communication [34].
Unlike traditional relay systems like Amplify-and-Forward
and Decode-and-Forward, passive RIS operates without heavy
power requirements, passively reﬂecting and phase-shifting
incoming signals. This enables environmentally friendly and
efﬁcient deployment. However, passive RIS technology faces
the challenge of “Double Fading,” resulting in signiﬁcant
signal degradation and reduced system efﬁciency compared to
direct links. To mitigate this limitation, active RIS designs have
been developed, enhancing overall performance by addressing
multiplicative fading [13].
2) Active RIS: Active RIS improves passive RIS technol-
ogy by actively amplifying and modulating the phase of
reﬂected signals with phase-shift circuits and ampliﬁers [35].
While active RIS systems consume more power, they convert
multiplicative channel fading into additive ones, improving
overall system effectiveness [36]. Despite concerns about
increased energy consumption, active RIS offers promising
cost-effective and efﬁcient solutions compared to traditional
relay systems [37].

B. Modes of RIS
RIS enhances wireless communications by manipulating
electromagnetic waves in three primary modes: 1) reﬂective;
2) transmissive; and 3) STAR. The reﬂective RIS directs
incoming signals back to the users located on the same
side of the BS. Transmissive RIS allows signals to pene-
trate, reaching users behind obstacles. STAR-RIS combines
both functionalities, managing signals in multiple directions
for complex environments. These modes improve network
adaptability and efﬁciency, catering to diverse communication
demands [40]. Fig. 3 illustrates the three operational modes of
RIS: 1) reﬂective RIS; 2) transmissive RIS; and 3) STAR-RIS.

It also modiﬁes the phase, amplitude, and other properties
of transmitted waves to ensure effective signal propagation
and coverage beyond the physical location of the RIS. This
implementation differs from reﬂective RIS, which redirects
signals back toward the same side of the BS, and hybrid RIS,

3) STAR-RIS: It is an advanced form of traditional RIS that
enhances signal coverage and adaptability by managing both
reﬂection and transmission of wireless signals [45]. In contrast
to traditional RIS, which solely reﬂects signals, it manages
users on both sides of the surface by dividing incoming
signals into reﬂected and transmitted components, thereby
offering 360-degree coverage [46]. This dual functionality
is valuable in complex environments requiring multiregional
signal management, such as from one room to another or from
outside to inside a building. However, its design and imple-
mentation involve challenges related to energy consumption,
system modes, and hardware complexity, which are essential
to address for fully exploiting its potential to enhance wireless
communication coverage [47].
The dual-mode capability of RIS technology signiﬁcantly
advances wireless communication by enabling networks to
switch seamlessly between enhancing signal transmission and
analyzing incoming signals [48]. This adaptability makes RIS
crucial for future systems to meet the intricate and evolving
demands of modern communication. The dual functionality of
RIS not only highlights its adaptability but also paves the way
for smarter, more efﬁcient, and responsive wireless networks,
marking a pivotal development in wireless communication
technology.

1) UAV as BS: UAVs functioning as aerial BS pro-

UAV BSs can offer temporary network connectivity in spe-

ﬂying cells to meet the increasing demand for connectiv-
ity [55]. In emergency situations or large events, UAV-BSs can
deliver rapid communication coverage, ensuring low latency,
enhanced power efﬁciency, and improved reliability [56].
UAV-BSs support advanced radio access technologies, such
as millimeter-wave (mmWave), free-space optical communi-
cation (FSO), visible light communication, and LiDAR. These
technologies are crucial for applications like augmenting con-
gested terrestrial networks, providing connectivity in disaster
zones, and optimizing communication in densely populated
areas [57].
2) UAV as Mobile Relay: UAVs deployed as mobile relays
signiﬁcantly extend network coverage by establishing or
enhancing communication links between BSs and GUEs,
particularly in scenarios where direct communication is
obstructed by physical barriers or long distances [58]. UAV-
enabled aerial relays are instrumental in wireless coverage
extensions, wireless backhaul, and emergency communica-
tion services [59]. Unlike ﬁxed relays, UAV relays can
dynamically adjust their positions to adapt to changing
communication environments, thereby optimizing network
performance [60]. UAV relays facilitate wireless commu-
nication between remote devices that lack direct links by
maneuvering ﬂexibly in 3-D space, thus overcoming obsta-
cles, such as buildings and hills, and enhancing overall
coverage [61].
3) UAV as Transceiver: UAVs as transceivers, or aerial
user equipment (UE), leverage existing terrestrial or aerial
networks for communication [62]. UAV-UEs share essential
operational data, such as altitude, ﬂight mode, and mobility
status with network operators, operating under constraints like
latency, stability, and throughput [63]. Due to their reliable
LoS connections, UAV-UEs face different interference sce-
narios compared to GUEs [64]. Ensuring robust and efﬁcient
connectivity for UAV networks poses signiﬁcant challenges,
including the need for advanced control and operational
technologies.
D. Overview of Edge Computing
Edge computing is a decentralized computing framework
designed to process data closer to its origin, minimizing
the need for extensive data transfer to centralized cloud
servers [65]. This framework consists of a layered ecosys-
tem, including extreme edge devices (such as IoT devices,
smartphones, and industrial machinery), localized nodes (such
as routers, gateways, and on-premises servers), and edge
cloud infrastructures (e.g., MEC servers, regional data centers,
and mini data centers) [66], [67]. These components collab-
orate to address key challenges, such as latency, bandwidth
consumption, and data privacy concerns, while enabling real-
time decision-making in diverse applications like autonomous
vehicles, industrial robotics, and smart cities [68], [69].
Unlike traditional cloud computing, which relies heavily
on centralized data centers, edge computing distributes work-
loads across these layers, optimizing performance. While
extreme edge devices handle basic tasks like data collection
and preprocessing, localized nodes process computationally
intensive workloads closer to the source, ensuring faster
response times [70]. Further, edge clouds provide scalability
and enhanced computational power, bridging the gap between
localized nodes and centralized infrastructure. This collab-
orative ecosystem supports both localized, partially private
networks and larger, interconnected systems, creating a robust
environment for scalable, low-latency processing [71].
1) Classiﬁcations of Edge Computing: It can be catego-
rized into two primary layers based on where computation
occurs:
Localized Edge: This layer processes tasks within private
or local environments, enabling low-latency responses and
efﬁcient task handling.
1) Extreme/Personal Edge: Refers to computation per-
formed on devices like IoT sensors, smartphones, or
industrial machinery, which handle basic, resource-
constrained tasks. This layer is crucial for initial data
collection and preprocessing [72].
2) Local Nodes: Includes intermediate components like
gateways, routers, and on-premises servers that man-
age more complex computations. These nodes act as
intermediaries between extreme edge devices and higher
level computing layers [71].
Edge Clouds: It represents the broader infrastructure that
complements the localized edge, offering scalability and
higher computational capacity.
1) Regional Edge: Consists of geographically distributed
data centers that handle advanced tasks while main-
taining proximity to the data source, reducing latency
compared to centralized clouds [67].
2) Cloud-Extended Edge: Includes interconnected MEC
servers, racks, and mini data centers closer to the data
source. These systems provide scalable solutions for
computationally intensive tasks and high-performance
applications [73].
This classiﬁcation reﬂects the interconnected and collabora-
tive structure of edge computing, ensuring efﬁcient resource
utilization across all layers.

enhancing security and privacy, optimizing EE, developing

1) Passive RIS is ideal for scenarios that require low-cost,

munication. These systems signiﬁcantly improve signal
quality, enabling reliable communication in complex
environments, albeit with higher energy consumption.

environments where both EE and high-performance
signal processing are required. This ﬂexibility allows
hybrid RIS to adapt to changing conditions, ensuring
optimal performance across diverse scenarios.

ﬂying operations, RIS reconﬁguration, and MEC tasks

needless diversions and keeping an ideal altitude that

quent connection instability. To overcome these issues,

environmental stressors while maintaining performance.

RIS units can help maintain stable communication by
adjusting to real-time changes. Future research should
develop predictive models to anticipate environmental
impacts and allow proactive adjustments to sustain
communication quality [28].
5) Mobility Management: Effectively handling the exten-
sive movement of UAVs is a considerable obstacle in
RIS-assisted MEC systems [136]. UAVs are intrinsically
dynamic, continuously altering their locations to include
various regions, adhere to predetermined paths, or react
to real-time occurrences. The ongoing motion has an
impact on communication lines, resulting in regular
ﬂuctuations in signal quality, interference patterns, and
connectivity status. Developing resilient mobility man-
agement methods that are specially customized for UAV
operations is of utmost importance [137]. The protocols
must possess a high level of adaptability in order to
promptly adjust to changes in UAV placements and
ensure the continuity and dependability of communica-
tion links.
6) Latency: Minimizing the delay for real-time applications
is a fundamental obstacle in implementing RIS-assisted
UAV systems for MEC. High-speed communication is
crucial for a range of applications, including real-time
video streaming, emergency response, and autonomous
navigation, where even little delays can have a substan-
tial inﬂuence on performance and efﬁciency. Moreover,
in dynamic settings, minimal latency requires real-
time monitoring and adaptability [138]. By constantly
observing network performance and the surroundings,
the system can able to identify and ﬁx such problems
before they affect the latency.
7) Resource
and
Trajectory
Optimization:
Joint
optimization
of
UAV
trajectory,
RIS
phase-shifts,
and resource allocation for MEC tasks is crucial for
improving EE and communication
quality. Recent
research emphasizes the signiﬁcance of building iterative
algorithms that integrate UAV mobility with RIS
setups to obtain maximum performance in dynamic
environments [139]. More work is needed to develop
more efﬁcient algorithms for real-time applications and
nonconvex optimization problems.
V. CONCLUSION
The integration of UAVs with MEC systems has sig-
niﬁcantly improved mobile network performance through
enhanced coverage, mobility, and data ofﬂoading efﬁciency.
Incorporating RIS into this setup further reﬁnes resource
allocation, optimizes system performance, boosts EE, and
enhances PLS. This survey thoroughly evaluates the beneﬁts
of combining UAVs and RIS within MEC networks, showcas-
ing advancements in computational capacity, task ofﬂoading,
and overall system performance. Our contributions include a
comprehensive overview of RIS, UAVs, and MEC, covering
various RIS technologies (passive, active, and hybrid) and
modes (reﬂective, transmissive, and STAR-RIS). We also
differentiate between UAV-mounted and UAV-enabled MEC
systems, and explore static (ground-based and ﬁxed array)
and dynamic (UAV-mounted) RIS conﬁgurations, as well as

Abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) have become essen- tial in advancing multiaccess edge computing (MEC), providing ﬂexible platforms that enhance network capacity, coverage, and efﬁciency while reducing latency and improving communication quality. Integrating reconﬁgurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) with UAV-based MEC systems further elevates these capabilities, deliv- ering signiﬁcant gains in computational power, energy efﬁciency (EE), and physical-layer security (PLS). However, managing the complexity of RIS within UAV networks requires sophisticated optimization strategies. This survey offers a comprehensive analysis of the fundamentals of RIS, UAVs, and MEC, followed by an in-depth examination of RIS conﬁgurations in UAV-based MEC systems, including static, dynamic, and hybrid models. We evaluate the beneﬁts and challenges of RIS integration, such as improved communication, enhanced computational efﬁciency, optimized energy use, better task management, and strengthened security. In addition, the survey explores the latest advancements in RIS-assisted UAVs for MEC, focusing on boosting computa- tional capacity, minimizing delay, maximizing EE, and enhancing security. To provide a thorough exploration of these topics, detailed summary tables are included, offering a comparative analysis of methodologies, performance metrics, and scenarios from recent studies.
